[/Azande_Baxter_1953_76_KS:p1] Today the most important duties laid on blood-brothers are to assist a man’s affines to dig his grave, and to contribute to the mortuary feast. If a man has to raise compensation for witchcraft, homicide, or adultery, a blood-brother must assist him; in the old days, when a man stood in danger of instant mutilation for the last offence, this help had to be immediate. Other duties, which have now largely lost their importance, were to warn the other if he had incurred the chief’s displeasure, and to assist at the post-mortem on a dead brother’s corpse, or the corpse of a kinsman of his. 57 There are occasional instances of one blood-brother being treacherous to another, usually by committing adultery with his wife, but such breaches are rare. The behaviour which blood-brothers are expected to assume towards each other is the opposite of that required towards kin and in-laws, and they stand to each other in a sort of joking relationship. They abuse each other with impunity, saying things that would normally be considered causes of deep quarrels. In a modified form this joking relationship is extended to clansmen, known as bakulemi; and between certain clans, such as the Abanvra, Abangombi, Akalinga, and Agiti, a permanent joking relationship has grown up. 58  1/3

[/Bambara_119_NK:p1] Joking Relationship A very important institution is also linked to the family name. It concerns the ties called “joking relationship,” dyo benatye (literally, agreement between us), which is integrated with the general kinship relationships designated in the Mandingo country by the term senãnkuya. But family relationships in the strict sense, called sindyi benatye (literally, breast milk between us), are to be distinguished from dyo benatye which, on the contrary, involves the members of two families, or even of two different peoples. Thus, a Koulibali is a Kéita's senãnku among the Bambara; Bozo and Dogon as well as Bozo and Somono are also senãnku(1). To the Mandé, a Koulibali and a Tangara, bound by a long and durable friendship, decided to seal it in a lasting way. They opened their veins and put a little blood from one wound into the other, thus realizing the alliance through this exchange. They next prepared a meal which they ate 84 together while pronouncing their oaths never to spill each other's blood. 1. Joking relationship called senãnkuya among the Bambara is termed măgu among the Dogon, dagana among the Bozo, etc. This
important institution, which embraces all the tribes of the French Sudan, has already been the object of a number of studies. See
especially M. Delafosse, Haut-Sénégal Niger /The Upper Senegal and Niger,/ Vol. 3, p. 206; H. Labouret, “La Parenté à plaisanteries en
Afrique occidentale /Joking Relationship in West Africa/”; D. Paulme, Parenté à plaisanteries et alliance par le sang en Afrique

quote: [/Chagga_Guttman_1926_305_KS:p1] Of all the salutation names with which the Chagga honors a member of an age grade none makes any reference to circumcision. The most important names refer to the period in the grove and to its secrets; all other names are borrowed from the sib organization. The most frequent salutation is ngoso: kafo ngoso as a greeting, nenga ngoso as a petition. Those who have been in the grove together use the terms rika and ngasi. The beseeching ma ngasi (blood alliance of the grove) constitutes a petition which the agemate cannot decline. But if a person is unable to give what the petitioner asks for, he protects himself against any further demands with the assertive oath: “mkombo ngasi.” Mkombo is the grove in which the Moshi people let their circumcised youngsters sleep during the last period. From the sib organization they took the terms mrata and toho. The members of the preceding age grades greeted them as wawa, wande, sahu, but also as msongoru (“the preceding ones”). Girls and women greeted coeval men with msatsa (brother), older men, however, with ndami (father of the husband). A mania for imitating and the tendency toward being regarded as something special are responsible for the changing fashions of the salutations of the age grades. When the influence of the Taita on the eastern slopes of the Kilimanjaro was great, the Chagga took over the Taita salutation, oro. In the Chagga and the Masai languages oro means he-goat. I do not know its meaning in the Taita language, but I presume it is the same. From the Masai the Chagga borrowed the salutation ndawo, which, among the Masai designates two booty-companions in the same age group. At the present time, a new designation for the members of the same age grade makes its appearance in the Kibosho district: momo, which in the Kibosho dialect means heifer. It started as a joking form of address among young men, and is now the fashionable word of Kibosho.  1/2
notes: Chagga borrowed a salutation from Masai designating two booty-companions in the same age group, indicating joking or playful interaction.

It is generally an insult to say to another WoDaaBe that he or she looks or behaves like a member of another ethnic group. Young men, for example, who stand in culturally defined joking-relationships (either in the same age group or cross-cousins) often refer to one another as Hausa or Tuaregs, intended then as a friendly insult. Too much association with members of other ethnic groups in the city is furthermore generally criticized and mocked. quote: [/Hausa_Smith_46_NK:p1] The affairs of Daura Throne slaves were important administrative and political agents in all Hausa and Fulani chiefdoms during the last century. However, to my knowledge, besides Fulani and Hausa Daura, only Hadeija allowed intermarriage between official slaves and the chief’s kinswomen. At Zaria, Katsina, Kano, and Sokoto, the ruling Fulani refused to allow their kinswomen to marry slaves. Apparently at Daura such marriages between the dynasty and senior slave staff antedated the jihad. Thus by recognizing such marriages, the Kuninkawa Fulani who ruled western Daura after Malam Ishi’aka’s death apparently adopted the practice of their Hausa predecessors. Kinship at Daura As remarked above, the Hausa of Daura stress agnatic descent and are organized in patrilineages of varying depth and extent. For the pagan Hausa or Maguzawa, patrilineages are also the primary units of social organization; but Maguzawa patrilineages are localized, exogamous, and differentiated  47 ritually by their relations with particular localities and spirits. Among Muslim Hausa and Fulani, lineages are neither exogamous nor localized, and cousin marriages are preferred. Following Islamic models, Fulani prefer to arrange marriages between brothers’ children, while Muslim Hausa prefer cross-cousin marriages of either type. In both the Fulani and Hausa kinship systems, cross-cousins are joking relations whose relationship involves privileged familiarity. Accordingly, Fulani and Hausa rulers like to appoint cross-cousins to their staffs, thus converting these warm and solidary kinship relations to political use. quote: [/tiv_12_nk:p1] The Tiv of central Nigeria HISTORY AND TRADITIONS OF ORIGIN TRADITIONS OF ORIGIN Tiv in almost all parts of Tivland say today that they came into their present country from the south-east. While they were “ coming down ” ( sen, that is, going north-west) they met the Fulani, with whom they lived for a time and from whom they parted peacefully. As evidence they cite the present “ joking relationship ” ( sengen ) between Tiv and Fulani. After leaving the Fulani, Tiv say, their forefathers had various adventures with the “ Bush Tribes ” before they finally emerged into the plains where they live today. Tiv postulate that long ago, when they were few in number, all Tiv lived in a single large community on top of a hill which they locate to the south-east. Just which hill this may have been is, however, a matter of dispute. Most agree that it was not Swem Hill (on most maps, Ngol Kedju in the Cameroons), but that they passed by Swem on the way down (and Swem holds a unique position in Tiv legend and religion). Akiga, and he gives a widely held version, says the hill was Ibenda, a hill with two summits in what is today Turan. There are several hills in Ikurav Ya (including Bar), which are said to be this original home in Tivland, while other equally knowledgeable elders in the southern areas claim that it was Iwokungun in what is today Takum District, Wukari Division. A few people in Kunav assert that this original settlement was on Ngokuv, a hill in Shangev Ya, but the majority say that the settlement on Ng[unknown]kuv was at a much later date and involved only one large segment of the Tiv, Jechira. People to the north and west, in Masev  1/2 ||| [/tiv_1_nk:p2] especially in southern Tivland, are as high as 1, meters. The undulating plains of tall grasses (as much as 3 meters high), dotted with savanna trees, lose elevation until they reach the Benue, at about to meters. The Tiv, who are an expanding people, are well along in their occupation of the similar plain that extends northward from the river toward the Jos Plateau. DEMOGRAPHY The earliest estimate of the Tiv population, in 1933, was , . In 1950 the count was about , . By 1990, the figure had climbed to more than a million. The density of population in Tivland in 1950 was about per square kilometer, but that figure is misleading. In the southern area, where the Tiv reside adjacently with the small groups of peoples they know collectively as the Udam, the density rises to at least 1, per square kilometer. LINGUISTIC AFFILIATION There is a single Tiv language intelligible to all, although regional dialects allow one to distinguish the area from which a person comes. The language is classified as the only example of its subdivision (on the same level as Bantu languages) of the Niger-Congo Language Family. HISTORY AND CULTURAL RELATIONS The Tiv say they emerged into their present location from the southeast. "Coming down," as they put it, they met the Fulani, with whom they still recognize a joking relationship. The earliest recorded European contact was in 1852, when Tiv were found on the banks of the Benue. In 1879 their occupation of the riverbanks was about the same as in 1950. British occupying forces entered Tivland from the east in 1906, when they were called in to protect a Hausa and Jukun enclave that Tiv had attacked. The Tiv said in 1950 that they had defeated this British force, then later invited the British in. The first British patrols of southern Tivland did not occur until 1911, which the southern Tiv refer to as the British "eruption." This year also marked the first arrival of Dutch Reformed missionaries from South Africa; they were joined, and then succeeded, by US Protestants in the 1940s and 1950s. Catholic missions arrived in the 1920s. ( 32 ) In the opening scene, Mai Samari reconciles a dispute between two members of the samariya who should have a jokingrelationship with each other ( wasan nangi ). Mai Samari draws out the example of different ethnic groups within Niger having a chain of such relationships with one another: Mai Samari: Haven’t you got that in your head? If he curses you, it’s not you he’s cursing. If you notice, if you go from here in the east to the west, our country is all one and the same. Listen to me carefully now. quote: [/Rwandans_Newbury_1980_395_KS:p1] But juxtaposing data from Rwanda and from Ijwi in this fashion produces a paradox: the Ishaza on Ijwi explicitly and universally deny Singa status, and people from all clans on Ijwi distinguish sharply between Mbiriri and Ishaza.14 Furthermore, the Ishaza have a joking relationship with the Mbiriri which differentiates them and maintains the differences between them.15 Moreover, on Ijwi ‘Jeni’ does not appear in the historical affiliations of the Mbiriri. The most plausible argument to explain this series of traditions is that Jeni, the putative ancestor of the Ishaza, was a member of a localized group which only later became absorbed within the more all-inclusive Singa identity to conform to Rwandan categories of social identity. This apparently occurred after the Ishaza and Mbiriri emigrations from Rwanda in the late eighteenth century, and thus corresponds with the period when Rwandan cultural norms spread through the area: it is primarily in the Rwandan traditions associated with the central court milieu that the descendants of Jeni are considered as ‘Singa.’ The apparent contradictions in these data then raise the questions of why, despite these apparent indications of common origins, the Mbiriri and Ishaza on Ijwi claim different status from each other and why neither calls itself ‘Singa.’ This discrepancy between the Ijwi data, which are clear and consistent, and the Rwandan claims can be explained by looking at the assertions of Rwandan associations as separate elements within an evolving process of clan identity formation. ethnique. C‟est le cas entre les Mossi et les Gulmantchéba du Burkina-Faso, entre les

quote: What the Mbuti liked best of all was a village that they took to be the best of the outside world, but with the least amount of pressure attached to it. There they put the classical joking relationship into action in a masterful way. Rather than bartering or trading, as villagers did, the Mbuti brought their kpara and karé ("brothers of the knife," village men with whom they had shared the nkumbi initiation) whatever they chose to bring by way of forest products, and did just as much work as they wanted to, in return helping themselves to whatever they wanted from their patrons' households or plantations.
notes: Text describes a culturally recognized, recurrent joking relationship between Mbuti and these village men.

quote: [/Luguru_McVicar_1935_63_KS:p1] The Wamangi are the watani of the Wambunga, and vice versa. The term calls for explanation in order to understand better both the joking relationship and cross-cousin marriage, of which latter infra. The singular of watani is mtani. Mtani is one of the two names by which a person calls his or her cross-cousin, the child of his or her mother's brother or father's sister, and by which he or she is called by him or her. It is by the same name, mtani, that you call a member of a sib which has the joking relationship with your own sib. Cross-cousins also call each other binam, but members of sibs between which the joking relationship exists do not call each other binam. In other words, cross-cousins may call each other either mtani or binam, but members of sibs between which the joking relationship obtains may call each other mtani, never binam. So far as I can see, mtani is a Bantu word, binam an Arabic one. Those who by reason of their sib joking relationship call one another watani may also be called wagongo, that is, those on whom one depends. When a person dies, it is his or her watani (of the sib with which his or her sib has the joking relationship) who look after the death rites. Thus when a death occurs the one sib depends on the other with which it has the joking relationship, and in this sense the watani are wagongo. Sibs between which privileged familiarity or the joking relationship prevails are said to kutaniana. The translation “joking relationship” may not be a first-  1/2

quote: [/Tallensi_Fortes_91_NK:p1] The dynamics of clanship among the Tallensi Quasi-Clanship: Joking Partnership Beyond the lineage's field of clanship lies a zone of social relations with which it has no constituted ties. For example, Zubiuŋ has no constituted ties with Zandoya. When Pal of Zubiuŋ abducted the young wife of a Zandoya man, this was his justification for an act which would have been considered an outrage if she had been the wife of a Ba'ari man. Again, when Sa□abo of Kpata'ar clandestinely brought home the wife of a Gorogo man, the elders of his lineage were ready to shield him. A few months later another youth of the same lineage eloped with the wife of a man belonging to a linked lineage, and the same elders peremptorily sent her home to her former husband. Somewhere between clanship and potential enmity come two other kinds of ties belonging to the same class of structural relations as clanship and generally accounted for as arising out of some form of kinship (mabiir(ə)t). Each clan among the Talis, and in some cases a particular maximal lineage, has one or more joking partnerships with other clans or lineages. Thus Ba'ari has a joking partnership with Gorogo, Zubiuŋ with Sakpee and Gundaat, Kpata'ar with Wakii, Degal with Samiit, and so forth. The natives describe these relationships in the following terms. They say, ‘We tease one another (ti kieh(ə)t ni taaba)’, or ‘We abuse one another (ti turc taaba)’. quote: [/Tuareg_Nicolaisen_1963_430_KS:p1] Ecology and culture of the pastoral Tuareg In spite of the application of the rules of joking relationship on a political level, troubles within the drum-group were far from unknown. And it is remarkable that even between the related tribes of Irawatten and Kel Azel there might be very severe quarrels. There was a latent opposition between them which might occasionally lead to fighting between noble Tuareg of the two groups. The existence within the drum-group of another noble tribe, the Kel Azel, with a certain number of vassals was always a danger to the position of the drum- chief as a ruler of the wholeKel Ferwan group. And noble Tuareg of the Irawatten tribe say that in the past it even happened that the drum-chief punished the Kel Azel very severely, not only taking all their livestock, but also burning down their camps. The drum-chief was able to maintain his power over the whole Kel Ferwan group because most vassal tribes were placed directly under his command, and because these tribes camped around Agadez which was dominated by him. The drum-chief also had trouble with another tribe of his group, the Kel Akerra. This tribe is said to have been originally of noble status and to have had as its particular vassals the Ibararojiten tribe. In the past the drum-chief assisted by vassals of the whole group imposed vassalage upon the Kel Akerra, who, however, refused to give him part of their bride-wealth.
